It’s time to say it: this game has no future.
You could go on about how "it's in Early Access" or "the developers are trying," but you hit the ceiling by the second playthrough—theoretically, you can even "beat" it on the first run (maybe not unlocking every single achievement, but still). There were plenty of minor features added over the summer, yet the game itself only vaguely reflects real stock market economics; company progression is very weak, and growth strategies are limited to just 7–10 options.
You can't really spend the money anywhere anyway (and why would you? When you're sitting on trillions, the only way to go into the red is through divorce... or prison). The only fun to be had is chasing numbers—setting personal bests, basically. Plus, the "80s Japanese trader" concept has limited room for growth on its own; it’s all too easy for it to devolve into a generic life sim—which, frankly, is already lackluster in this game. I have no idea what the developer could possibly roll out next. Right now, it’s a game that lasts an hour—maybe two. Nice pixel art and... that’s it? There’s no real thrill to the trading, either. If it gets a full release or things change a year from now, I might change my mind, but for the moment, that’s where it stands.

At first glance this game may seem boring, being an investor in the 80s Japanese stock market doesn't sound super compelling at first glance. But once you start the game you quickly realize the game has far more depth then it seems, and its continuing to get better and better with each update. Generally, if you like making tough decisions, strategy, but also cozy vibes, then you will probably have a great time.

In the game as you make your character you decide some starting traits, and then as you play you choose which stocks to buy and when, figuring out the right time to sell those stocks, you can also run your own business, start a charity and more, there are decisions you can make that alter how you play as well, you have many different ways to play and get presented with many different routes to go down.

I do think companies need an overhaul, but that's honestly my only gripe, the game is solid and very enjoyable and I look forward to where it goes from here!

Ya know... since [b]Stonks-9800[/b]'s announcement, I had always had a [b]feint[/b] interest in this title... if for little other reason than its visual and audio aesthetics. Something about its [b]gorgeous, yet simple, color palette, combined with its peppy-upbeat music selection[/b] reminiscent of the old Japanese PC-9800 Computers wicked soundchip [b]really[/b] drew my attention. But what [b]actually[/b] made me pull the trigger on this purchase so soon was the absolute dog-s#%& behavior of Sony and their blatant disregard towards the smaller developers who make the very industry they survive on grow. So my statement [b]STILL[/b] stands...[b]F#%& you Sony.[/b]

But you know what's interesting about all this? What [b]started out[/b] as a purchase simply made in spite of another company, turned out to be one that opened my eyes to an avenue of genre I didn't know I could like, and even more so...[b]find a newfound love & appreciation for![/b] Stonks-9800 has that [b]"certain special something"[/b] that manages to [b]pull you in and hold on tight[/b], keeping you coming back for more even if you have absolutely no f#$%ing idea what you're actually doing! Don't get me wrong, the game isn't perfect. Its [b]not exactly beginner friendly, and their doesn't seem to actually be any real tutorial[/b]. So if you go into this one with no prior knowledge of the stock exchange...well then[b] good f$%&in luck! It's gonna be trial by fire![/b] But even so, learning through this method is....actually part of Stonks charm! Even when you're learning, make mistakes, and go into crippling debt, Stonks somehow [b]still[/b] finds a way of presenting it all to you in a colorful, fast moving, and upbeat pace. Which lets you know you're still financially f#%^ed...[b]but in a fun way![/b]

Look, I don't even know what the f$%& I'm getting at either, all I know is this... 

Regardless of my initial reasoning for purchasing this title, [b]Stonks-9800's addictive gameplay, phenomenal music, and captivatingly charming theming, outshine and surpass it.[/b] The love and passion that goes into this title is very apparent, and it would do a great disservice to let that be overshadowed by anything else. This game in many ways finished possibly five or six updates ago, but TERNOX being the chad he is decided to make his dream game come to life with even more updates, addons, in-depth mechanics to essentially build the paradise and subsequent hell of 80's Japan bubble-economy madness. 

I say the above as when it was in 'early' early access it already felt rather well built for its release, and had some rougher edges but coming back to it time and time again and finding the new substantial updates has very much made it into a sandbox life-sim that I guess also has stocks as the driving narrative. Buy low, sell high, see the company you've been sailing on plummet to nothing because of terrible management decisions (like real life :0), buy a ♥♥♥♥ car that burns in a horrific fire every six months, have your apartment go the same way, make it all back because another company just soared on the loan you just took out while also winning that blackjack hand you needed--then subsequently have it all get taken away in just one pachinko game. 

This game honestly has it all, you can make your fortune on many different markets, whether you're buying metals/oil/property for the long-con, or just riding the stock market on 3x speed hoping to sell at just the right time or hodl as much as you can. The stock market is as gamey or real as you want it to be (I suggest just playing on the realistic settings as it really is the definitive experience). This isn't even mentioning the life-sim aspects of having to manage stress, getting plastered with friends to deal with stress, playing golf with friends to deal with stress, dating Amy to deal with stress (still waiting for that romance update TERNOX DAMN), and the many other city romps that help enhance the image of being a degenerate stock broker in Japan. Now you can marry people too for zaibatsu shenanigans but not AMY YET TERNOX, DAMN.

This isn't even mentioning the whole Yakuza underground aspect where you can make some solid cash before possibly getting killed by same Yakuza because you accidentally sold that stock you were holding for them because of a bad pachinko run. 

Anyways, masterpiece of a game. Would buy three times over (already bought it twice here and on GOG) if it means TERNOX is forever chained in the basement making new updates.

[table]
[tr][td][b]❗Status[/b][/td][td]In Progress; Paused for Updates (Early Access)[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][b]🎮Played On[/b][/td][td]SteamDeck Only[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][b]⏱️Game Length[/b][/td][td]12.6 hours in. Still a lot left to see, especially as updates come out.[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][b]🔄Replay Value[/b][/td][td]High potential. The stock system, life sim mechanics, and company building all have a lot of room to grow, and the game is still in active development. I will absolutely be coming back as updates arrive.[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][b]💙Favorites[/b][/td][td]💬 PC-98 Aesthetic Done Right: The whole game leans into the look and feel of 80s and 90s Japanese computing, specifically a PC-98 art style with anime-style character portraits, a CRT-like color palette, and low-res retro energy running through everything. The music fits, the old Toyota-looking cars you can buy fit, even the interface fits. It commits to the bit fully.

💬 Actually Learning Stocks: I have no background in stocks and this game has enough depth that I started to genuinely understand how they work. That is an accomplishment for something that is also just fun to play.

💬 The 10-Hour Unlock: Around 10 hours in, you can finally start your own company, and a lot opens up at once in a great way. The patience to get there is worth it.

💬 Watching the Days Go By: There is something really relaxing about letting time move in this game. The rhythm of the days cycling, a year passing before you notice. It is calm in a way that is hard to explain but easy to feel.
[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][b]🛠️Improvements[/b][/td][td]💭 Gift Economy Needs a Store: The friendship system is fun but getting good gifts relies too much on random events and the crane game, whose prizes are mostly nods to other fandoms that characters do not seem to actually care about. A shop where you could buy gifts with intention would make the social layer feel a lot more purposeful.

💭 Balance and Bug Pass: A few things need tuning. Fish occasionally glitch into walls during fishing and become uncatchable. Pachinko losses feel extreme and consistently discouraging. And I lost 3 cars in a single year to back-to-back accidents, which suggests the odds may be off.

💭 Charity System Onboarding: The upgrade flow, where you need to level up the charity first and then spend that level as a point on an upgrade, is not explained clearly in-game. A brief tooltip or intro would save a lot of confusion.
[/td][/tr]
[tr][td][b]🎯Verdict[/b][/td][td]Recommended, with the caveat that this is early access and still finding its edges. Stonks 9800 has a fully committed PC-98 aesthetic, a stock system with depth, and a slow-burn progression that opens up significantly once you can start your own company around the 10-hour mark. Easy mode still managed to bankrupt me multiple times before I turned a profit, which I found more funny than frustrating. Rough edges worth fixing include the gift economy, a few balance and bug issues, and some systems that need better onboarding. I also hope story mode eventually digs into Amy and the bar lady's storylines, because those friendships feel like they are building toward something. More feminine Japanese name options in character creation would be a welcome addition too. I have paused for now but will absolutely be back as updates come out. If you like life sims, retro Japanese aesthetics, or idle games with surprising depth, keep an eye on this one.[/td][/tr]
[/table]

As if things aren't bad already, you end up crashing your car so badly you end up with a paperweight instead of an automobile, and you can't follow through on certain opportunities because you have no way to get to them. Then, that trip to the bar that your friend insisted you go to, because you were rather stressed, gives you food poisoning and you can't make it to a meeting to buy a couple thousand cheap shares from a solid company that someone more desperate than you is selling for a whopping 30% discount.

What do you do next? Go to the pachinko parlor and think to yourself "Maybe if I hit it big here, I can get my money back and fix this mess!"... Well, guess what? A couple of minutes later you see yourself out of money and options, pondering what your next move should be. "Oh well", you think to yourself, "these things happen and now I have to deal with this situation the best I can." At the end of the day, at least there are games like STONKS-9800 to keep your mind off the setbacks and just relax a little.


[spoiler] In all seriousness though, if you're into tycoon/economy games, you should buy this game, you won't regret it. (Considering you have enough money after the pachinko shenanigans, that is...) [/spoiler]

I bought this game on a whim expecting a dry spreadsheet sim. What I got was a fever dream set inside Japan's legendary 1980s economic bubble — and I haven't left my desk in three days. STONKS-9800 nails something most financial games don't even try: it makes getting rich slowly feel absolutely electric.
The loop of scraping together your first hundred thousand yen, watching your hand tremble over the buy button on a blue-chip stock, and then — yes — seeing it surge as Japan's economic miracle keeps on miraculing... it's genuinely joyful. The game captures the era with loving fidelity. The music is a synth-drenched banger. The UI looks like it escaped from a Sega Saturn. The ticker tape never stops moving.
The real magic is the career trajectory. You genuinely feel the climb. Every stage of the journey has its own texture — the scarcity of early trading, the thrill of your first corporate investment, the surreal power trip of the late game when you're not just buying stocks, you're buying companies.
Becoming a CEO isn't just a title screen — you're managing a company, making real decisions that ripple into the market you're also trading in. The moment I realized I could crash a competitor's stock price by timing my own press releases, I let out a cackle that scared my cat.

Now, fair warning: the endgame is where things get a little quiet. Once you've climbed to the summit and the Nikkei is basically your personal instrument, there's not a ton left to chase. The sandbox loses its teeth. You're not grinding anymore — you're just... existing at the top of a mountain, watching numbers go up on autopilot. For some people that's satisfying in a Zen kind of way. For me, it was a gentle signal that the credits were spiritually rolling.
But here's the thing: I don't care. The grind is the game. The thrill is in going from scrounging for yen to casually acquiring Shibuya real estate. STONKS-9800 is one of those rare titles where the journey is so well-crafted, you almost don't want it to end — which makes the slight emptiness at the top feel earned rather than lazy.

STONKS-9800 is a VERY aesthetically pleasing game. 
Unfortunately it feels like there is very little to do (I'll get to why it is like that later), even though there are many systems/side activities that bombard the player at the beginning.

Artstyle and soundesign/soundtrack are amazing, it's straight up vibe. Honestly it feels way more immersive than what you can see in a trailer. The developer cooked with this one.

The biggest problem is how repetitive the gameplay loop is. After maybe 2 hours of game time it feels like everything repeats every single week. The progression is super slow and of course rng but I somewhat understand that, its supposed to be a stock simulator, but the "simulator" part isn't there. This is more of a life sim than a stock simulator, which would be fine if the "life" part also wasn't so repetitive and shallow. I do like interactions with Amy and the bar girl (forgot what her name was) but there also isn't much you can do with them. Amy at least gets events that happen once in a while and are something new and fresh. The "normal" interactions are starting to repeat very soon after just a few months playing and they are always just listening to what the girl has to say. Interactions with generated friends and connections are boring. There are a lot of minigames like golfing and fishing that fit the overall experience but it never feels satisfying in the long run. 

As for the economic part of the game, it's boring and straight up rng. Player often gets "tips" and "hints" on things that are happening inside the traded companies, car manufacturers or info about real estate, but it's always like "I overheard someone talking that X company is doing good" or "Things are going well" or "Things are going bad". It ends up being a 50/50 gamble what will happen, if we trust that this happens like that or not. The game theoretically makes it possible to befriend board members/CEOs and such of traded companies but you can't really extract any useful information from them, at least from my experience. Earning money is tedious, the only reliable way is to get a normal job offer once the player is low on money, and meanwhile have 2 days to trade in a week.

All the game mechanics are shallow... too shallow, it really feels "wide as an ocean deep as an puddle".

You may ask me why did I decide to leave a positive review if it is boring and my answer would be that I had fun, even though I was super bored. I was vibing but I can't bring myself to play STONKS anymore. It feels super grindy and player just waits for something to happen to him once an hour, it doesn't feel rewarding to think and plan, because the player 50% of the time gets rewarded with bad rng.

This game is cheap, if you want to vibe I recommend you buy it, if you want to play an actual stock market sim or a life sim, then don't buy it, because its just slow and tedious. It's a deja vu game, where every hour of gameplay feels like it the previous one repeats. Soundtrack/sound design/graphics are 10/10, for me gameplay is at most 5/10.

Here is my review after playing Stonks-9800 for around 20 hours.

This game is basically filled with gambling elements in almost every detail. From the main gameplay loop of trading stocks, to mini-games, to the Charitable Foundation system, everything involves risk, randomness, and decision-making. You can run a charity, invest in art, buy real estate, invest in small projects, or even call different people. Many actions can lead to different outcomes, which makes the game feel very dynamic.

One thing I found very interesting is the horse-racing mini-game. You can literally gamble your entire net worth. The game does not limit how much you can bet. If you want, you can put down one thousand billion in one go. There are also other mini-games, such as gacha, claw machines, and even fishing. During holidays, you can go fishing and upgrade your bait to catch different types of fish. The whole game is full of gambling, leverage, upgrades, and dopamine hits.

Speaking of leverage, it is not only used in stock trading or short selling. You can also use leverage in your charitable foundation activities. For example, you can organize events with 25x leverage. This makes the game feel even more chaotic and exciting.

The information flow in this game is extremely fast. By the mid-game, there is basically a news message popping up every one or two seconds. What makes it special is that the game keeps running even when you open other windows. News messages will continue to appear and spam you no matter what you are doing. The pace is very fast. You are constantly making decisions, gambling, earning money, and then spending it on things like cars and real estate.

One design choice I really appreciate is the “Buy It All” feature. For example, when buying real estate, you do not need to purchase each building one by one. You can buy all available buildings at once and upgrade them together. This makes the game much smoother and avoids the tedious process of clicking “Yes” again and again.

That said, I think the game could still do more with relationship development. For example, each character has a Friendship value. When that value reaches the maximum, it would be interesting if special relationship events could happen. Maybe the player could develop a romantic relationship, a secret affair, or even create messy office drama.

The locations could also be expanded further. For example, adding hotels could make the world feel more like a mature adult society. It would also make the gameplay more complex, deeper, and more interesting overall.

Money is a mystery to me. I don't understand how it relates to value, and investments are even further removed from the core concept of intrinsic value. I don't know what a dividend is. I have absolutely no idea what I'm doing in this game. I don't know if I'm doing things right or setting myself up for catastrophic failure in the future. Is it better to own 2% of a once-failing company or just sell off the shares for tremendous short-term profit? Diegetic time is zipping by at an alarming rate and I feel like my virtual life is slipping past me without much progress.
...And yet I keep coming back. This game is oddly compelling and slips into my mind unexpectedly.

I don't understand it, but I think I like it, so maybe you will too.

Considering how many games on steam are just low quality simulator games with just enough content to be considered a game and constant updates to the game to make it worth your while I had very little hope for this game going into it. But after spending about 30 minutes in the game I felt like I was playing one of the best simulator I’ve played in quite a long time. From the style to the gameplay loop to the overall feel and high replay ability I feel in love with this game. The games style does a really good job at matching a Japanese 80s feel with it’s pixel art style and attention to detail with stuff like cars, the town, and in game NPCs interests and jobs. It’s very simple and requires you to do a lot of reading but it really makes you feel like a stock broker in 1980s Japan. It’s loop maybe a bit boring, repetitive and too luck based for some but this is a game about stock investing so I’d consider it to be very accurate to real life. The addition of a part time job and the guy who gives you stock info for a price give you a good safety net for when your first investment opportunity shows up (even if the latter lies to me half the time). You also have many ways to make money you dont have to make it with just stocks. You can make it with real estate, deposits, dividends, commodities, your own personal company, investments into company prototypes, and buying art. This mixed with its high amount of personal bonuses you can choose at the start of your game makes it a game that can be played multiple times without getting stale. Not to mention this game gets updates very often any time there’s a slit bug that impacts the game and major updates every 1-4 months with a shocking amount of content that appears for the time period. Overall I absolutely love this game for accurately portraying the stock investor experience and for the dev for being so committed to his game. I’m excited for the full launch of the game and will probably be voting it for indie game of the year when it comes up.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
9/10: Dang making money and hoarding real properties, cars, and artwork is awesome. I also love that assistant Amy. The new girl Sae (the bartender) is pretty good-looking, too. This game really captures the spirit of 1980's Japan, and not just with the third console generation graphics. The only downer is that the game doesn't give enough pointers, and despite the name of the game, the player will be making most of their money through gambling instead of stocks.

[h1]Overview[/h1]

Despite the name [i]Stock Trading Oriented Network and Knowledge Simulator[/i] (or simply [i]STONKS-9800[/i]) the game primarily isn't about trading stocks. Instead, the player will mostly find themselves going to either the panchinko hall or the racetrack to make lots and lots of yen. The player is well advised to buy stocks once they can afford to wait on making a profit with all of that great inside information. (Or fortunes, if the player was intelligent enough to start the game as a fortune teller.) After amassing enough wealth, the player should start their own non-profit organization so that they'll get some benefit out of money that will otherwise be going to pay taxes. Once the skill-related charity boosts are all purchased, then the player should go ahead and start their own company, and then boost their net worth through stock ownership. (Even if the player chooses to never sell their stocks.) Fun, right?

What's the point of making money if you cannot spend money? There's many types of homes to buy in five different areas, and the player can even choose to live in one if they so wish.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3701700277

Apart from homes, there's also business properties to purchase to make passive income, artwork (which usually depreciates), and cars. (Which absolutely depreciate.) Despite what happens to artwork and cars, the player is well advised to purchase a lot of both due to numerous achievements to earn.

[h1]Graphics and Sound[/h1]

Both the graphics and the sound are straight out of the third generation of consoles. Fortunately, the player has Amy to look at, which the player will absolutely want to be doing!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3672470093

Now there's a bartender named Sae to also look out, which isn't quite as likeable to ol' Il Pallino, but dang, anime girls can be so perfect!

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3696627400

The sounds and music are all straight out of the third generation of consoles. The music loop sets the mood, but depending on one's interest (or even tolerance) of game music from the era, the background music can get annoying after awhile.

[h1]Positives and Negatives[/h1]

The reason this category is grouped together, is because in spite of the name [i]Stock Trading Oriented[/i], the player will be making most of their money from gambling. Panchinko is almost a guaranteed payday and horse racing became a bit more difficult to pick the winner after it was modified to have more information to influence the outcome. More than anything, the player seems discouraged from trying to make money from stocks because it can take weeks to buy up all of the remaining shares. (As well as sell all of the remaining shares if the player is trying to cut their losses in a downturn in stock prices.) The important thing is that games are meant to be fun, and making money in [i]STONKS-9800[/i] is hella fun!

What's the point of making money if you can't spend money? The player will be expected to buy themselves a car so that they can drive to business deals or even go out on weekends and holidays if the player's friends all say no. (Amy can offer to keep the player company.) Eventually, the player will need to buy themselves an entire fleet of automobiles just for the sake of earning achievements. (As well as making a grotesque display of wealth.) Housing can also be purchased, which can help the player's mood if the housing is good enough. (After awhile, the player will likely just buy housing so that they can rent out the property, though this earns far less compared to buying out commercial properties.) There's also even art to buy up, which isn't interesting for the most part. (And mostly depreciates in value.) But the player should absolutely amass an art collection for the sake of hunting achievements.

Although the mini game for golf is a nice, casual experience, the game gives no clue to the player as to what they're supposed to be doing in the karaoke mini game (it looks like pressing directional arrows, and sometimes even holding down a directional arrow) and ol' Il Pallino was caught totally off-guard. More than anything, it looks like all of the NPC's in the game are better singers than golfers! Ol' Il Pallino was also caught off-guard the first time it came to making a speech at a stock shareholder's convention. No information was given about how the player should have their fingers concentrated on the "G," "H," and "J" keys. Although the speech mini game is easy enough to do well in (without being perfect) and making a speech can even cause the company's stock value to rise even if the CEO's speech doesn't go over well with shareholders.

For better or for worse, the bar room is a double-edged sword. The player will want to go to do things like get information on horses from Sae, play blackjack against Sae for some pretty cool bonus items, and meet other people. Go to the bar too much, and the player won't be able to decrease their stress as much. Go to the bar way too much, and the player will need treatment for alcoholism, never mind the fact that the player is normally going to go to the bar with an ulterior motive other than getting drunk.

[i]STONKS-9800[/i] doesn't do enough to clue the player in on what they should be doing. Just so the player knows, the player should start with found their own charity after earning enough money. After all of the [i]scholarship[/i] upgrades have been purchased, then the player should see about starting their own corporation.

The stats system is interesting. Not only does increasing stats not only drop achievements, but they provide the player with numerous benefits, and they impress Amy!

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

[i]STONKS-9800[/i] is a strong buy at every price. This is one of the top tier games that involve making money, so go make that money!

Stonks 9800 is an absolute gem for anyone who loves strategy, finance sims, or that nostalgic late-90s PC aesthetic. The game perfectly captures the chaotic energy of market speculation while still delivering surprisingly deep and rewarding mechanics. Every decision feels meaningful — whether you’re timing a risky buy, diversifying your portfolio, or riding the wave of a volatile surge.

The gameplay loop is fast, addictive, and layered with complexity. It’s easy to understand at first glance, but mastering the systems takes real thought and planning. Watching your investments climb (or crash!) creates genuine tension, and the satisfaction of pulling off a well-timed move is incredibly rewarding.

Visually, Stonks 9800 nails its retro-inspired presentation. The UI has personality, the sound design adds to the immersion, and the overall atmosphere really sells the fantasy of being a high-stakes market mastermind.

If there’s one feature that would elevate this game even further, it would be an in-game option to easily customize and change company names to your liking. Being able to personalize the market with custom company names would add even more immersion, creativity, and replayability.

Overall, Stonks 9800 is a stylish, smart, and highly engaging simulation that’s easy to recommend. With just a bit more customization, it would be near perfection.

[h1]STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator – Early Access Review[/h1]

[b]Game:[/b] STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator
[b]Genre:[/b] Financial Simulation / Strategy / Satirical Sandbox
[b]Status:[/b] Early Access

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Introduction – Charts, Chaos, and Capitalism[/h2]

STONKS-9800 is not just a stock market simulator—it’s a chaotic interpretation of financial obsession wrapped in retro-futuristic presentation. It blends serious trading mechanics with exaggerated market volatility, meme culture energy, and a surprising layer of psychological pressure.

It asks one simple question:

[i]Can you survive the market… emotionally?[/i]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Core Gameplay – Risk, Reward, Regret[/h2]

At its core, STONKS-9800 offers:

• Real-time simulated stock market fluctuations
• AI-driven corporate behavior
• News events that impact markets
• Shorting, options, leverage systems
• Portfolio management tools
• Random “market anomaly” events

The game walks a line between realism and satire. Some mechanics feel grounded in real trading strategy, while others lean into absurd volatility spikes and dramatic crashes.

This balance makes it engaging—but occasionally unpredictable in ways that feel more chaotic than strategic.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Strengths – Where STONKS-9800 Shines[/h2]

[h3]1. Emotional Feedback Loop[/h3]

The biggest achievement of STONKS-9800 is how it captures the feeling of trading:

• The adrenaline of watching green candles surge
• The dread of a sudden red cascade
• The regret of selling too early
• The arrogance of holding too long

The UI reinforces this with audio cues, subtle heartbeat effects during major losses, and increasingly aggressive news headlines as volatility rises.

It’s immersive in a uniquely stressful way.

[h3]2. Retro-Futuristic Aesthetic[/h3]

The “9800” theme carries a nostalgic late-90s tech vibe:

• CRT-inspired overlays
• Neon graphs
• Over-the-top financial news tickers
• Synthetic background music

It gives the game personality beyond spreadsheets.

[h3]3. Sandbox Freedom[/h3]

You can play conservatively… or become a reckless leverage gremlin.

The systems allow:

• Slow portfolio growth
• High-risk day trading
• All-in gambles
• Market manipulation attempts (within mechanics)

That freedom gives the game strong replay value.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Weaknesses – Early Access Rough Edges[/h2]

[h3]1. Balance Inconsistencies[/h3]

Some market events feel too swing-heavy. Sudden 80% collapses can happen with limited warning, making certain losses feel scripted rather than organic.

Early access patches have addressed extreme volatility—but tuning is still ongoing.

[h3]2. Tutorial Clarity[/h3]

The onboarding is currently one of the weaker elements:

• Complex mechanics are introduced quickly
• Options trading lacks deeper explanation
• Risk management systems could use clearer UI prompts

New players may feel overwhelmed.

[h3]3. AI Market Logic[/h3]

While marketed as AI-driven, certain market patterns become predictable after extended play sessions. Advanced players can identify repeatable behaviors.

This doesn’t ruin the game—but it limits long-term depth until expanded.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Early Access Handling – Transparent but Still Stabilizing[/h2]

One of the most important aspects of any Early Access title is communication.

STONKS-9800’s developers have shown:

[b]Positive Signs:[/b]
• Regular patch notes
• Active community polls
• Public roadmap visibility
• Fast bug hotfixes
• Balance adjustments based on player feedback

[b]Concerns:[/b]
• Roadmap goals occasionally shift
• Feature delivery timelines sometimes slip
• Performance optimization patches are inconsistent

The developers appear engaged—but the scope of their ambition may be stretching resources thin.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Community Sentiment[/h2]

Current player sentiment trends toward:

• Positive for concept and atmosphere
• Mixed for balance consistency
• Cautiously optimistic for future depth

Many players appreciate that the developers are listening. The tone in community forums suggests trust has not been broken—but expectations are rising.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Emotional Experience – The True Hook[/h2]

STONKS-9800 is not just about profit.

It’s about:

• Greed
• Fear
• Impulse
• Patience
• Hubris

It simulates psychological trading traps surprisingly well. Watching your portfolio balloon only to crash minutes later feels devastating—even in a game.

Few simulators capture the emotional volatility of markets this effectively.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Longevity Potential[/h2]

If the developers:

• Refine AI market behavior
• Expand corporate event systems
• Improve tutorial onboarding
• Balance volatility more organically

STONKS-9800 could evolve into one of the more compelling financial simulators available.

Its core foundation is strong.

The question is whether Early Access momentum sustains.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict (Early Access)[/h2]

[b]Concept & Identity:[/b] 9/10
[b]Gameplay Depth (Current State):[/b] 7.5/10
[b]Balance Stability:[/b] 6.5/10
[b]Early Access Communication:[/b] 8/10
[b]Atmosphere & Presentation:[/b] 9/10

[b]Overall (Early Access): 7.8/10[/b]

Stonks 9800 has an incredible aesthetic, but very little of it actually comes together.
The game absolutely nails the 80s PC-98 anime vibe. Character creation is charming, though the pixel art is all over the show some is lovely other parts are amateurish. But the idea of a retro stock market life sim is genuinely exciting.
Unfortunately, almost everything beyond the visuals, and music feels underbaked.
Despite being a stock trading game, you have almost no meaningful way to influence the market. Prices fluctuate wildly with little logic or feedback, and most “information” you get, rumours at the bar, networking perks, even insider tips, either do nothing or actively punish you. I took multiple networking and social perks, assuming befriending CEOs or corporate boards would provide stock tips, early access, discounted shares… anything. It doesn’t. You can drink or golf with the CEO of Sony, but it has zero gameplay impact.
This is the core issue: nothing feeds back into the main game.
There’s a lot of content here: fishing, golf, arcade shmups, karaoke, gachapon machines, cars, property, art collecting, socialising – but almost none of it matters. Fishing has hundreds of fish… that do nothing. Arcade games give no rewards. Gachapon collections are pure filler. Cars range from broken trucks to billion-yen limousines, yet function identically. Property investments cost hundreds of millions for laughably tiny returns. Even perks like “Psychic” amount to vague fortune-cookie messages that don’t affect gameplay.
Early game, this lack of systems actively hurts the experience. With no reliable way to make money, you’re often locked out of large portions of the game. If you do get lucky and snowball, money quickly becomes meaningless anyway. Starting a company sounds exciting, but it’s also poorly balanced, shareholders will demand things well beyond your first year is possible and are wildly unrealistic, I.e. get your HR department to 75% efficiency requires upgrades 4 times the cost of the making the business.
The game feels like a collection of half-finished ideas rather than a cohesive system. It’s as if the developer wanted to make a fishing game, then a golf game, then a pachinko game, but never tied any of them back into stock trading. Compare this to something like Persona 5, where side activities directly strengthen the core gameplay. Here, side activities just… exist.
Is it fun? Not really.
Is it addictive? Unfortunately, yes – number-go-up brain chemistry still works.

I'm hopeful for Early Access improvements, but right now it feels more like busy work than meaningful additions.

In the early stage, you slowly build your fortune through stock trading — every yen counts. You’ll find yourself betting on horse races, playing pachinko, watching every market movement, and managing your relationships carefully. 

As long as you catch the stock and real-estate booms before 1989 and 1992 (the years when Japan’s real bubble burst), you’ll get to experience what it truly feels like to be rich.

But later on, everything changes. Money becomes meaningless — just numbers on a screen.
I stopped trading stocks and buying property altogether; my companies were making so much profit every month that I couldn’t even spend it all. I ignored phone calls, went out only with my assistant, and started wasting time on gacha machines (500 yen per spin), even though a single stock trade could easily earn me 500 billion yen.
That’s when I realized — being too rich is actually boring.

Overall, this game perfectly captures the rise and fall of economic ambition.

Welcome to story time:
Invest all your money into all stocks on the market equally. Cry in your apartment because you don't have a car to get to the stock market. One of your friends invites you to the Pachinko Arcade machine where I strap into my chair HONOR bound to bring home the money. Walk in with less than 1 million and walk out with more than 14 Billion. Invest into stocks, apartments, houses, cars, art, and start a questionable telecommunications company called CumCast where the only the thing that comes faster than our technicians is you. Only hire 4 people to sit at the board room thinking that will be enough to run a good business. Let one month go by and lose 1 billion from the new business and another loss in the stock market. Go to my company where I very intelligently hire 1 manager for production and  force him to make every new product or commit Sudoku! At this point I'm broke when I get a brilliant investment idea. I take my last 100mil and head to the Pachinko parlor and lose my first 40 million. I go back in this time determined to not lose my next 40mil.

So after losing 80 million Yen you'd probably assume I would pull back and invest in a stable commodity like gold, oil, silver, or maybe copper. That's why your reading my comment and not living the fast life in 1980s Japan. I took the last 20 million and head right back to the Pachinko parlor and walk out with 42 billion Yen.  It's at this point everyone is impressed with my financial success and I get a book written about my genius investment strategy.

Anyways one year later CumCast stock is worth 40k Yen and the next highest is Calio at 30k Yen. At this point I sell off 90% of my stock in CumCast and wait for the price to drop. It's been two years and CumCast stock is worth over 130k. I still don't know how to run the business but at this point I might never be able to reinvest into CumCast.

Was it worth it? Yes. What Came first? Yes. Should you Come into the world of Stonks? Yes!

[h1]An experience in an experience[/h1]

It is a curious game. Very diverse. There is a LOT to do combined with a retro design for less than 10€. It is a no-brainer just buy this. 

You will start with buying stocks but soon you will discover the joy of pachinko and then the secret poker parties.
Once you buy all the stocks of a few companies you will decide to create yours, financing it by collecting rent and reselling your art collection for a profit. If you are in a bad position your ties with the yakuza will help you out... or not (they seem to have a different definition of what is a good deal in real estate, I bought too many haunted houses because of them). 
With the last update you were introduced to the joy of creating your own charity organization, a way to give back to the community while paying less taxes. But does the community really need all this? You can embezzle money. You will be voted the most influential figure in 1985 Tokyo and will siege in every firm's board deciding of their fate. 
Living a very stressful time you will be a huge donor of next door temple to apaise your mind... or go to the bar to hear the last business rumor. Finally you will spend all your money in the arcade trying to finish your collections or be on the leaderboard.
If you want to take a step back from city life you can take a vacation and go to fish. Which is a fully developed game too.

All in all STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator is a game collection in a game with retro design.

STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator, developed and published by TERNOX, is a retro-inspired financial simulation game that transports players to the dazzling, neon-lit world of late 1980s Japan. It’s a game that revels in nostalgia, drawing aesthetic inspiration from PC-98-era interfaces and economic bubble culture while mixing the addictive thrill of stock trading with the humor and eccentricity of indie game design. Beneath its parody title lies a surprisingly engaging experience that blends satire, strategy, and simulation into a compact, entertaining package.

At its core, STONKS-9800 is about making and losing fortunes. Players take on the role of a young investor navigating a simplified version of Japan’s stock market, buying and selling shares across a variety of fictional companies while keeping an eye on personal well-being. The goal isn’t just to amass wealth—it’s also to maintain a balance between profit and sanity. Stress, hunger, and fatigue are just as important as market trends, and neglecting them can derail your success as easily as a bad investment. This fusion of life simulation and trading mechanics gives the game an unusual but entertaining rhythm: one moment you’re analyzing stock graphs, and the next you’re unwinding at the bar, buying sushi, or testing your luck at horse races and pachinko parlors.

The gameplay loop is simple yet engaging. Market data updates dynamically, forcing you to decide when to hold your shares, when to sell, and when to risk everything for a big payout. Real-world logic applies—buy low, sell high—but the game’s humor and unpredictability ensure that luck often feels as important as skill. Your choices affect both your finances and your stress levels, with each in-game day presenting new temptations, random events, and small narrative touches that make the experience feel alive. The charm lies not in realism but in how the game captures the spirit of speculation and greed from Japan’s bubble economy era, all wrapped in a tongue-in-cheek presentation that pokes fun at capitalist excess.

Visually, STONKS-9800 nails its retro aesthetic. The entire interface is designed to look like a late-’80s computer terminal, complete with pixel fonts, chunky icons, and the muted color palette of early financial software. It feels authentic and playful, like a forgotten simulation dug out of an old hard drive. The music amplifies this atmosphere with upbeat city-pop-inspired tracks and jazzy background tunes that perfectly evoke the optimism of the era. The result is an experience that is as much about style as it is about substance. Even when the markets crash and your portfolio burns, it’s hard not to smile at the absurd charm of its presentation.

While the simulation aspect is enjoyable, the game does have its limits. The systems are intentionally lightweight, offering enough complexity to stay engaging without ever becoming overwhelming. Players looking for a deep, realistic economic simulator may find it too shallow; the markets lack real-world intricacy, and some patterns can feel predictable after extended play. The side activities, while fun, can grow repetitive once you’ve seen their outcomes several times. Still, this simplicity is part of the game’s identity—it’s less about mastering algorithms and more about enjoying the ride, embracing both the humor and the chaos of capitalism distilled into pixels.

The game’s accessibility adds to its appeal. It’s easy to pick up, runs smoothly even on low-end hardware, and can be enjoyed in short bursts or longer sessions. The developer’s clear affection for the PC-98 aesthetic and Japanese economic culture shines through in every detail, from the humor-laced item descriptions to the nostalgic sound effects. It’s a love letter to a specific time and place in gaming and economic history, presented through a lens of modern irony. The inclusion of small achievements, collectibles, and visual flourishes gives players reasons to return, even if the core mechanics don’t drastically evolve over time.

STONKS-9800 ultimately succeeds because it understands its audience. It’s not trying to teach financial literacy or simulate Wall Street precision—it’s trying to entertain through absurdity, style, and charm. The mix of stock trading, personal management, and minigames captures the addictive loop of risk and reward, all while laughing at the very idea of getting rich through “stonks.” Its world may be small, its systems simple, but its personality is enormous. For players who appreciate retro aesthetics, tongue-in-cheek humor, and the thrill of chasing profits in a digital bubble, it delivers a surprisingly compelling and memorable experience. It’s a satirical yet affectionate take on greed, luck, and ambition—a reminder that, sometimes, the most rewarding investments are the ones that don’t take themselves too seriously.

Money is not wealth. It is a system of control, born in debt and shackled to interest. For every U.S. dollar that exists, five more in debt demand repayment — a treadmill that can never be stopped, only sped up. We do not pay off our debts; we pass the burden in circles, a society forever chasing numbers where balance is forbidden by design.

In 1862, Abraham Lincoln issued the greenbacks, interest-free government currency to fund the Civil War without bowing to bankers. In 1865, he was assassinated, and the greenbacks were buried with him. In 1930s Germany, a failed Austrian painter introduced interest-free credit to pull his nation out of collapse. For a brief moment, money served the people instead of the financiers. But this experiment too ended in ruin, crushed by global war and by the powers that profit from debt.

The story repeats across history. In 1881, President Garfield warned that whoever controls money controls the nation — weeks later, he was gunned down. In 1963, John F. Kennedy issued Executive Order 11110, allowing silver-backed currency to bypass the Federal Reserve. Months later, he was assassinated. In 2011, Muammar Gaddafi pushed for a gold-backed African dinar to free the continent from the dollar system; NATO forces intervened, and he was killed in the desert. Even Andrew Jackson, who fought the Second Bank of the United States in the 1830s and for a moment paid off the national debt, saw his “victory” followed by the Panic of 1837, which threw the nation back into financial bondage.

Every attempt to escape the system ends the same: silenced leaders, ruined nations, or crises that restore the status quo. It is as if debt-money defends itself, striking down anyone who dares to imagine money as a tool of freedom rather than a weapon of control.

Enter "STONKS," the theater of speculation where we pour our wages and hopes into shares of debt-laden companies, mistaking paper promises for wealth. The market rises, it falls — and we celebrate or despair — yet all the while we remain tethered to a system designed to keep us running in place.

The question is not whether you are winning at "STONKS." The question is whether the game itself was ever meant to let you win.

STONKS-9800 is everything it says on the package, and so much more than you can imagine. I picked it up thinking I might refund it, and I was hooked almost immediately. As a real-life trader, I was curious how a game could capture the thrill and chaos of the stock market. STONKS-9800 surprised me with it’s simple, retro, and unexpectedly addictive gameplay.

🕹️ Retro Vibes & 80s Japan Setting
Set in 1980s Japan, the game greets you with pixel art and old-school menus. You start by creating a character—not the most advanced customization system, but that’s not the point. Then you choose your difficulty level and how historically accurate you want the market simulation to be. This matters, because every economic event affects stock prices in ways that feel eerily real.

💼 Traits, Capital, and Strategic Depth
Depending on your difficulty, you’ll be given a starting investment fund. Then come the traits—each one gives you unique advantages and disadvantages, shaping your playstyle. From there, you begin your journey as a rookie investor trying to make it big.

🎮 Gameplay That Sucks You In
The retro visuals might turn some people off, but the gameplay? It pulls you in fast. I told myself I’d play for 30 minutes… next thing I knew, hours had passed. Watching a stock you picked skyrocket is pure dopamine. It’s the kind of thrill only traders truly understand.

🏢 From Investor to CEO
The game doesn’t stop at buying and selling. You can become a CEO—either by founding your own company or buying enough shares to take control of an existing one. Every decision you make affects your company’s stock price. And yes, the game even includes short selling, just like in real-world investing.

📈 Realistic, Yet Risk-Free
This game nails the feeling of investing—strategizing, reacting to market shifts, and watching your portfolio grow. But here’s the best part:
Real life investing: spreadsheets, anxiety, and existential dread. STONKS-9800: buy high, sell low, laugh anyway. It’s the only market crash that feels fun.

✅ Final Verdict
STONKS-9800 may look simple, but it’s packed with depth. The retro aesthetic fits the 80s setting perfectly, and the gameplay is so addictive it’ll have you coming back for more. It’s the only place where I can invest recklessly and still sleep peacefully at night.

I have a fiendish addiction to games that exist to occupy a fraction of my time. Line go up number fests that make every neuron in my decrepit skull turn on through nothing but sheer benign overstimulation. Cookie Clicker fragmented a part of my psyche back in middle school and I've never been able to outrun the lasting damage it did. So naturally something like STONKS-9800 made sense. The generic business management sim is a market that is either cripplingly unfun Capitalism II style games, or ones that exist to beat you over the head with a brick like Space Warlord Organ Harvesting Simulator. Sitting in the small area of business management and activating my neurons is STONKS. All of the business fun with enough other things packed on to accurately recreate being a business man in 1980's era Japan except I'm not losing as many fingers to the Yamaguchi-gumi.

STONKS places you in Japan, 1980 in a tiny apartment with a bit of money to your name and you must masterfully take advantage of stupid dividend returns, real estate investment and legitimate gambling to become a financial mogul. Your means of getting there manifested through a few token character traits and a slowly expanding roster of stats that allow you to become a master of short selling stocks into the floorboards. Because if you REFUSE to give me my desired buyout, I'm sending your company to Izanami with express delivery. This is already a good framework for a business management game, but STONKS doesn't stop there. Kitschy Famicom graphics and eyesearing color palletes are only the start of various systems that make this an accurate representation of 1980's Japanese life. You must also manage YOURSELF. 

Balancing your four humors of financial well being (phlegm), social well being (red blood), mental well being (black bile) and relations with your secretary (yellow bile) is important to success. Being an insane loner hoarding stocks can get you into the market, but once you have a full company you need to consider more things. You need to take breaks lest you get sent to the hospital, you need to take friends of yours out to drinks and pachinko to get better benefits like insider information and recruitment into the eventual company you'll own. And if you think Amy is just a piece of eye candy to draw in mediocre horny bastards, that's false. That woman is one of the best people you can have for your company if you level relations up enough to get her involved, and she hands you market advice and business deals on a silver platter. She is as important to your financial success as honest means of financial advancement are, such as being a yakuza stoolie and winning apartment leases through smashing the "all in" button. This game is not immune to the Poker Night At The Inventory school of thought. And now I own a house!

The bread and butter that sells STONKS is the meta mechanics, and the various little side games tucked in between the hyperfixation with lines going up. At any point you can elect to just stop doing stock broking and drag an unfortunate friend into a whole host of minigames. Force that mediocre haiku poet to sing 24 Kan Cinderella, make him bet 2 billion yen on a horse named Suzuki Jimny, or go to the pachinko parlor. You will not regret going to the pachinko parlor and somehow turning 50 balls into 1503 because you zoned out and kept mashing the space bar. The game is really good so far. It can take a small bit to get going and to know what you're doing, but once you find a strategy it's super fun. It really gets me thinking and it makes me feel quite immersed honestly. I also really enjoy Amy and think she's an especially nice touch on top of some really good game-play.

This said, there are still a lot of glitches that I hope get patched out in the future. There also a fair amount of tiny things that I hope get improved on in the future.

Examples include: ~When I talk to the Yakuza, the color palette changes from what I set it too. This happens so often it's honestly quite an annoyance, especially since you have to go through every color to change it back to what you like. I wish there was a way to just set the palette and not have it change at all. I understand why it'd change when you talk to them, however with everything else I just stated, if it can't be fixed so it changes back to previous settings, I think it'd be better if the palette just remained the same no matter who you talk to. 

~ There are a fair amount of visual glitches, which don't get in the way of game-play too often but are still quite off-putting, such as during horse races, where if you press the escape key to make it go faster, sometimes the horses will run off screen after crossing the finish line. I also had an instance where Amy tried to talk to me right as I went to the horse race and she was covering the majority of the race screen until it was done.

~ I enjoy the ability to speed up time, however with how slow saving is, in combination with how Amy tends to disrupt game-play when telling you something (i.e: giving you your monthly report.) It unpauses and can often led to disruption. I'll often be trying to buy stocks before the market closes when she pops on screen and then I don't get the chance to continue until the next day. Which isn't too bad, but it is still a mild annoyance.

~ I wish there was a way to buy stocks in bulk, as it can be a bit cumbersome to try and buy stocks in bulk, especially when you have gotten to a point where you are rolling in cash and are just trying to continue that flow. I know it's a very minor thing, but I figured I'd state it since it did bother me a small bit.

~ I also wish that you had more access to the general Yakuza services as it feels like they're out of service more often than not. It feels like you get to use it once a year and then that's it. I understand this is to balance things out, however I think it'd still be nice if you could get to use these services at least two times in one year, as in my opinion I think that'd be fair and not cause too many game-play issues.

Overall this is a really good game and is a load of fun. I'd recommend it to anyone who enjoys these kinds of games and wants something to occupy themselves with for a while. I'm excited to see what else the developer does with this title. I'm also really excited for when the story-mode gets released. :)

[h1] Great game with amazing graphics and concerned developers. [/h1]

[h2] Introduction [/h2]
I started playing this game because of Game Grumps. I instantly fell in love with it. The mini games are fun and the different types of investment are very cool. The game is very natural at punishing those who don't diversify and it is great at modeling how volatile the market is.
This is still in early access and there are a lot of quality of life still to be done, but the developers are very concerned about this. We can see through the updates' history that QoL is taken seriously.
The CRT graphics are the best I've ever seen. It truly mimics how it used to be in a way that isn't ugly or tiresome to the eyes.

[h2] About the game [/h2]
[h3] Investments [/h3]
The game offers several ways to invest and make money. You can go to the stock market directly, buy real estate, buy commodities, short sell, create a company and put money on independent projects. All of these are affected by how the economy is going, and there are several factors that you must look into before investing. You can be ethical or not. It is all up to how you want to reach the top.
[h3] Personal life [/h3] 
You have a personal life in this game. There are three main stats: [b] Happiness [/b], [b] Comfort [/b] and [b] Stress [/b]. They are not independent and affect each other. Being too stressed or too unhappy might create bad situations for you. Sickness, not being able to give a speech to shareholders and stuff like that.
In your personal life you also have friends, including your assistant, Amy. You can call them, invite them to go out and send them gifts. These friends can become good sources of information or employees for your company. You can also just have fun with them. There is no need to use people.
[h3] Mini games [/h3]
The mini games are SUPER FUN. They aren't jenky like most mini games, they are usually quick and straight to the point. Some mini games can help you with social relationships like getting gifts from the arcade claw machine.
[h3] Achievements [/h3]
The achievements are good, but need to be tinkered some more. They can get really annoying when they require random stuff like getting a rare toy or fish to appear. The pachinko one, specifically, takes way too long. Aside from minor bugs common to early access games, this is the thing the devs should work more on.

[h2] Conclusion [/h2]
If you enjoy tycoon type games, this one is for you. There are many strategies for you to choose and you can carve your path to success the way you enjoy the most. Live your best life in the 1980's Japanese stock market.

[hr][/hr]
[h1]What is STONKS?[/h1]

    STONKS-9800: Stock Market Simulator is exactly what it says there on the cover. It is of course, a game, so expect some whacky stuff you wouldn't expect in real life (though not too whacky).

    In this game, you create your own character and play as them. There are not a lot of customization options, at least in appearance, but you do get to choose among perks that may help or hinder you (or both) for your playthrough.

    You spend most of your time looking through different management screens / interfaces. These screens are mostly graphs for the market price of different stocks and commodities as well as sheets detailing different companies. You also get interfaces for your character's status and profile as you do have to manage your character's well-being as part of the gameplay. As you play, there will be prompts that explain various news about the conditions of the different companies, as well as your character's well-being.

    Perhaps I'm making it sound a little too boring, but note that there are also multiple mini-games to be found. There's a fishing mini-game, a claw-hand mini-game, a pachinko mini-game, a poker mini-game, a golf mini-game, and so on. But mostly, yes, most of the gameplay is about watching lines go up and down and then rushing to go buy or sell stocks. There is a prevalent theme of chances / gambling as this permeates through the selection of mini-games (notice how they are all chance-based with the exception of the golf mini-game).

    Finally, there is Amy, the mascot you see on the front, and there seems to be an under-implemented dating-sim mini-game (?). Of course, the game isn't finished developing, but there seems to be a groundwork for that. The game makes no shortage of notices for when you improve your relationship with her, your advisor.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Evaluation[/h1]

Disclaimer: I do not have any experience trading, nor have I ever worked as part of a financial institution, so I cannot give a definitive evaluation of the accuracy of this game regarding the stock market's volatility.

[h2]Graphics[/h2]
(7/10)

    As I have expressed in the first sentence of this review, I adore the graphics of this game. Maybe it's just nostalgia, but I love how the graphics are curved as if I was viewing this in an old-school CRT monitor. I also love the developer's choice to make the graphics pixelized. Something about these design choices make me feel like an old-school professional in the late 80's / early 90's. 

    On a less enthusiastic note, the character profile picture and the NPC's profile pictures are all using reusable parts (I mentioned earlier that the game has character customization). Unfortunately, I find this part of the game less appealing. I wish this part would get remade. This is in sharp contrast with Amy, who has detailed art down to the midsection, [strike]just above the knees[/strike]. I understand this game is in development, but seeing Amy this detailed makes me wish there were more people with more "character" in the game. Some minigames also leave something to be desired, particularly the fishing mini-game and the horse-betting mini-game. I understand that these were meant to give off a retro video-game feel, but I feel as if these can still be improved without stepping over that.

[h2]Music[/h2]
(6/10)

    The music is great as well. The game goes through seasons. Every time I am just about to be sick of the current background music, the season changes, and the music changes along with the interface. The music is kept fresh and I appreciate that.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
(6/10)

[h3]No Handholding[/h3]
    As someone who did not have prior experience to trading, I found the gameplay interesting. At the start of a new game, you create a character with some short-descript perks, and then you are dropped into the management screens with no instructions on how to proceed. That's how I like it. I like a game that doesn't hold my hand, but has that option when I need it. It is a game where you explore what you can do. That last screen in the game is the "Advisor" screen which is where you can talk to Amy and there is an option to get hints. She doesn't really say anything about click here or click there, but rather, because this is a simulator, she tells you the general idea of how real-world ideas are projected in the game. For example, she tells you how to get "reputation" and what you can do with "reputation".

[h3]Skill Issue..?[/h3]
    With that said, majority of the game is looking at lines go up-and-down. And sometimes, you just let it do that for a solid few minutes. This is for when you want to earn money with dividends (money earned passively per month from the companies you have invested in). Fair enough, since this is a simulator, it may just be a skill issue if your gameplay is mostly that. The game doesn't encourage nor discourage you from just endlessly waiting on your dividends. Of course, there is always a possibility that the company that has your investments goes bankrupt, but like I said, this is a game where you explore what you can do. It's up to you if you want to make bold moves or safe moves. I like that about it. I said before that I am interested as someone who has never touched the stock market and that is because I can safely touch that experience with a simulator such as this.

[h3]Mini-games[/h3]
    To break up that experience however, there are mini-games. I find that these games do a good job at being palette-cleansers especially since they are varied. Some of these mini-games are unlocked as you go through the game, so the game doesn't throw this all in your face at once. Some of these games can actually have an impact in the main gameplay, particularly pachinko and poker. In these games, you can earn large sums of money or in the case of poker, assets such as real estate. And of course you can take huge losses in these as well. Other games have collectibles and the game graciously helps you keep track of them. Unfortunately, most of these games are still just the same gambling or chance-based calculation gameplay as the main game. After a while, they too can get tiresome. It would be nice if there were other types of games, though as it is, it's fine. Personally, it gives me a natural point for taking a break from the game.

[h3]Other[/h3]
    As I have mentioned, there seems to be an underdeveloped part of the game with Amy. I am honestly interested in that and wish to see more in the future.

    Another thing I would like to see improved is the interactions with the NPCs. As it stands, I barely go into the contacts screen to bother talking with the NPCs. I also don't see the point of bothering to improve my relationship with these people. For now, that contact list just keeps getting bigger and harder to keep track of without any reward for it. I suppose I'm just supposed to feel good about being popular? I might just be missing some hidden gameplay since I'm only 9 hours in, at the time of writing.

[hr][/hr]

[h1]Summary[/h1]
(6.3/10)

    STONKS has very good potential. As it currently is, it is already fun for me, someone who has never entered the stock market scene before. The interface is nice and nostalgic, as well as the music. If you enjoy looking at multiple different screens to optimize resources, this is the game for you. However, if you're looking for blood-pumping action, interactive NPCs, or realistic graphics, better look elsewhere.

★★★★★ "An 80s Stock Market Fever Dream for Aspiring Tycoons and Strategic Madmen"

Stonks-9800 is a hidden gem, a tactical sandbox disguised as a pixel-art finance sim.
It looks like vaporwave anime nostalgia—but underneath that simple UI is a brutal, addictive simulation that rewards real-world investment logic, risk management, and long-term strategic thinking.

You start off small.
Buy some stocks.
Collect dividends.
Lose it all.
Claw your way back.
Reinvest.
Diversify.
Speculate.
Dominate.

I went from broke to running a real estate empire pulling 15% monthly ROI, while simultaneously manipulating markets and planning my own company.
The dopamine loop is insane—but so is the level of tactical thinking it demands.

It's not a "game"—it's a capitalist initiation ritual.

🔹 ART & SETTING:
Retro Japan vibes? Perfectly nailed.

The minimalist UI actually enhances immersion—it's like reading financial software from a neon-lit Yakuza office in 1986.

It’s not about flashy design. It’s about depth. And Stonks has it in spades.

🔹 STRATEGIC DEPTH:
You’ll learn about dividend yield, market cycles, asset allocation, and real estate investing without realizing it.

There's a real psychological game here—do you chase growth or stability? Can you stomach a crash?

Every mistake teaches you. Every victory feels earned.

🔹 VISION & POTENTIAL:
This is where it gets wild.
The game already feels alive—but the potential is monstrous:

Add analyst tools, forecasting dashboards, insider rumors.

Expand the world: illegal deals, Yakuza interactions, shadow markets.

Maybe even cybercrime modules or economic warfare mechanics.

A dark underbelly of finance that pulls you deeper into the 80s corporate underworld.

You could turn this into the Dwarf Fortress of finance games if you keep building on it.

And let’s not forget—Ternox coded this while living in a literal warzone. That alone earns full respect.
The man is building a masterpiece under fire. He has all my support.

🔹 VERDICT:
This game doesn't just simulate markets. It simulates the mindset of a hustler.
If you like systems, strategy, numbers, and slowly becoming a god-tier finance warlord—this is it.

I learned more playing Stonks-9800 than I did reading investment blogs.

The developers have really spent some time working the aesthetics of this game and have done it well.  It feels like one of those old “executive series” NES video games like Areobiz 1 and 2.  Even the music hits just the right tone for that style of game and it is obvious the composition was well thought out.  The CRT screen bend is just noticeable on a regular monitor, and even more so on the steam deck.  Down to the three red green blue dots of the CRT screen.  The amount of time spent working on the sound, like the old DOS computer fan spinning up and old mechanical had drive clicks.  The attention to time specific aesthetics is well done.

I didn’t really want to believe in the reviews I saw before I bought it.. Can it really be that addicting?  Yes, it can, and again well made.  A few early access bugs but you see an update from the developers a few times a week.  Some disappear, some new ones show up, but in general it’s a solid progression of getting even fewer and fewer bugs.

I bought this game on sale… but I would also pay full price for it… if it’s not on sale, still worth a grab!

Aesthetics and updates are only one part though, I have seem many games with great bones but they also need lots of work…. This one doesn’t need that much work for it’s quality of life, user interface, and the game balance also has had plenty of care of attention and play-testing.  The stocks do function like stocks, historical mode or random mode.  You can make appropriate bets on stocks and not worry about the math being messed up in the background.  The odds of that stock going up or down, and should you go short or long, those calculations simulate real life close enough for this game and they enhance the experience.  I love buying some company just on the edge knowing it could go bankrupt… or I could net 10% of the company at a firesale prices.  Some games that still need more work, I would't do that becasue the outcome would already be known... here, it could go either way.

Bugs seen in the past few weeks.  

Noted on the Steam deck my cursor will not go fully to the edge for the top or bottom menu UI features.  Swap between controller or mouse can increase functionality, but that update has pushed me back to PC to play, this is a very recent change so I expect a fix soon.  (update between Jan 19 and Jan 22)  Though I can toggle between controller and touchpad (mouse) on steam deck... press the A button and it defaults back to controller.  

Poker has a few odd hands, ties being calculated not quite to the same texas hold’em rules I am familiar with.  High card, or kicker seems to be off.  The AI is competent enough in poker though some odd decisions on their part but nothing terrible.  To their credit, poker is a hard game to program AI players for so, well within reason for early access and the poker room is playable enough.  

Companies not traded on the current market keep getting news blurbs, though sometimes they show up as IOP’s some just never show up.  I usually just imagine these companies being under another index I’m not trading in.  

So far the bugs are minor, and the developers are frequently applying updates.  Not only does this game have bones of something amazing, it's very functional in it's current state, something we can't say about other early access games.  

Why I keep going back to play.

I keep seeing another goal in front of me, not only are they obtainable after an hour or few hours of game play but there are lots of options how to get there.  It has a great sandbox mentality to it and lets the player grow the story around their experience.  That is what makes a game stand out and be replayable.

Update:  The issue with the cursor on the steam deck not reaching the top or bottom menu bars, fixed within 96 hours since my post.  

I also noticed, the AI players can be bluffed in the poker mini game, that is not easy  to program so well done.  I also caught the AI player trying to bluff me!

As someone who works in the finance industry and wanted to make a market sim. himself, I would like to provide some valuable feedback to the devs. which I feel will make the game more interesting:

Having a balance sheet, income statement and cashflow statement for all the companies would be a great addition. Instead of meeting people at the bar and hoping for information on stock price movement, having few financial ratios and fundamental metrics will make for a more interesting play.

While it may seem daunting to the new players to have so much information bombarded at them, the charts would move as a function of both the stock's metrics from the financial statements as well as the insider tips from bars, resulting in a richer gameplay.

Interest on bank loans and charity donation should be tax-deductible because I didn't face any real penalty for being extremely unethical. This would allow players to use debt as capital expenditure to upgrade their own company. A company with bad debt/equity would be more volatile and susceptible to adverse market movements.

Players should be given an option to use leverage, with the tax deductible debt and option to leverage, the players will have more bandwidth to siphon funds from the exchange to their own companies and result in more interesting plays. Each stock could be given a real 'Beta' as a volatility indicator, this makes sure that the market isn't heavily skewed to 1 stock, as this happened with my playthrough with 'Hardbank'.

These are a few additions I believe would make the game more interesting to play, but it is absolutely a solid game and I've had a ton of fun playing this. Really hope the devs. see this, you've been doing an amazing job!
